$comment: Data-driven slate definitions. One LoRA fine-tune on the 20-layer base serves every depth: needle build --lora merges the adapter and then slices the rung, so `layers` here is an export-time number, not a training one (needle/model/finetune.py:293 `rung`, model/build.py). `labels` is the variant's class scope: it filters both the rows (answers[0].name) and the tool catalogue the rows carry, so a 3-class variant is trained against a 3-tool grammar rather than told about a class it cannot emit.

variants.description: Smallest rung, full 4-op label set. The latency play: 4 of 20 layers, expected to be the fastest archive on disk and the one most likely to trade per-op recall for speed.
Middle rung, full 4-op label set. The rung finetune/Makefile ships by default (LAYERS=8), so this is the variant production would run.
Full-depth rung, no slicing: the accuracy play and the upper bound for the two smaller depths, at ~5x the weights to load and quantise.

Scope variant: triage only (leave vs nudge vs flag), trained and decoded against a 3-tool catalogue. declare_done is out of scope because the mined corpus has zero targets for it (mine/decision-points.ts labels never map to it), so the class cannot be learned from this data and only widens the grammar.

Control, not a fine-tune: the published base checkpoint sliced to 8 layers with no adapter. It costs one `needle build` instead of an epoch, and it is the row that says what the fine-tune would have had to beat — the zero-shot baseline at the shipped depth.
